newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Stakes high for Nigeria and Abacha in Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Stakes high for Nigeria and Abacha in Sierra Leone.

text.p: Nigeria's credentials as the regional power in West Africa and a myth surrounding military ruler General Sani Abacha are at stake in a confrontation with the Sierra Leonean rebels and soldiers who took power in a coup last month.
Analysts and diplomats said the near humiliation on Monday of Nigerian forces trying to restore ousted Sierra Leone president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah was bound to inflame the situation.
"Nigeria's standing is at stake but so is Abacha's own reputation and future," said political commentator Joe Adigwe.
"If we win, respect for Nigeria will soar, but be prepared for recrimination and all that goes with it if we lose."

Nigerian forces acting under the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) of which Abacha is chairman began shelling Freetown at dawn on Monday after failing to persuade the soldiers who ousted Kabbah on May 25 to restore him to power.
But the operation went wrong for them when a Nigerian force guarding a hotel sheltering hundreds of people was overwhelmed by rebels.

The new Sierra Leone government says about 80 people were killed in the attack. Reporters in Freetown said Nigerians, who previously were considered "big brothers" by Sierra Leoneans, were now loathed in the city.

The rebels took prisoner 300 Nigerian soldiers and 13 of their officers at the hotel and threatened to use them as human shields at military areas that could be targets for any new Nigerian bombardment.
But it backed down on Wednesday and released them all in what they described as a goodwill gesture ahead of talks with West African negotiators.
This eased the immediate problem for the Nigerians but did not solve the dilemma for a force which came to Sierra Leone to promote peace, not to fight Sierra Leoneans.
"The planning of this whole thing does not particularly inspire confidence and now the Nigerians have to try to salvage their reputation," said one African diplomat in Lagos.
Nigeria has flown more troops and equipment to Freetown and has made clear the mission to restore democracy in Sierra Leone will not be abandoned.

"We will continue on the path we have set, meaning that there would continue to be consultations among West African leaders until the legitimate government is restored," Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi told BBC radio in Harare where he is attending an Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit.
The summit ended on Wednesday, pledging support for efforts to restore democratic rule in Sierra Leone.

"We unanimously agreed on the setback to democracy...and we call for the restoration of the constitutionally elected government," Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe, the new OAU chairman, said in closing remarks.

His words will be a big morale boost for Nigeria and Abacha, an infantry general who himself took power in a coup in 1993 when his predecessor annulled a presidential election that would have restored democracy to Africa's most populous nation.

His relations with the West have been tempestuous over his slow democratisation moves and alleged human rights abuses including the continued detention of Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled vote, and the 1995 hanging of nine minority rights activists in defiance of world opinion.

"If Aso Rock (the seat of power in Abuja) accepts to fight military dictatorship abroad it will also be compelled to reject same at home," said Bola Akinterinwa, editorial page editor of the independent Thisday newspaper.
"This will also compel the Abacha administration to democratise within the time frame provided for in the transition to civil rule programme," he added.
Analysts said pressure on Abacha to keep to his promise to hand over in 1998 will build up after the Sierra Leone debacle.
This appeared to have begun in Harare on Wednesday when the OAU called for a return to democracy in Nigeria and Burundi.
"We are getting tougher and tougher each time. I can assure that for future coups, it will be much tougher," Mugabe told a news conference.

A campaign by his friends that Abacha should stand in next year's election and become a civilian president, which opponents say is the hidden agenda of his transition programme, will also come under more scrutiny.
"The myth that Abacha is the invincible general is under test in the Sierra Leone," commented the African diplomat.
